title: Theories of International Relations
hook: Why do states behave as they do? Three big theories give rival answers — and which lens you use changes what you see in every global event.
key_points: Realism: states are self-interested actors pursuing power and security in an anarchic world.
Liberalism: cooperation is possible through trade, institutions, and shared interests.
Constructivism: ideas, identities, and norms shape what states want, not just material power.
Each is a lens — together they explain more than any one alone.
content_html: Faced with the same world events, experts often disagree sharply about what is really going on — and a large part of that disagreement comes from the theoretical lens they use. The study of international relations is organized around a few major theories, each offering a different answer to the basic question of why states behave as they do. Knowing the three main ones gives a toolkit for analyzing any global event.
extra_html: Realism is the oldest and starts from the anarchic structure of the international system: with no authority above them, states are self-interested actors who must look out for their own survival, so they pursue power and security and treat conflict as an ever-present possibility. For realists, ideals matter less than the hard calculus of power. Liberalism does not deny anarchy but argues that it need not mean perpetual competition: states share many interests, and trade, international institutions, and interdependence can make cooperation rational and war costly, so the world can become more peaceful and rule-governed over time. Constructivism shifts the focus from material factors to ideas: it argues that states' interests and identities are not fixed by power and geography alone but are constructed by history, culture, norms, and shared understandings — so that what counts as a threat or an ally can change as ideas change. Encyclopaedia Britannica surveys these and related schools as the main frameworks of the field. None is simply "correct"; each illuminates real features of world politics that the others underplay, which is why analysts often draw on more than one. The value of knowing them is that they make your own assumptions visible — when you explain an event, you are usually, knowingly or not, reasoning through one of these lenses.

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

related.title: Soft Power & Hard Power
related.hook: States get their way two ways: by force and money, or by attraction. Knowing the difference between hard power and soft power explains a lot about how influence really works.

related.title: The UN & International Organizations
related.hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.

flashcards.prompt: What is the core claim of realism in international relations?
flashcards.back_html: States are self-interested actors pursuing power and security in an anarchic world with no authority above them.

flashcards.prompt: How does liberalism differ from realism?

choices.text: It argues cooperation is possible through trade, institutions, and shared interests
It claims power is the only thing that matters

flashcards.explanation_html: Where realism stresses competition for power, liberalism emphasizes that institutions and interdependence can enable cooperation.

flashcards.prompt: What does constructivism add to the picture?

choices.text: Ideas, identities, and norms shape what states want — not just material power
Only weapons and money determine state behavior
States have no interests at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Constructivism argues that interests aren't fixed by material facts alone; shared ideas and norms shape how states define them.
